name: Elena Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Elena, 27, and I'm the lead loader operator at an underground zinc and lead mine. A loader underground is a long, low machine that scoops up the blasted rock and carries it to the ore pass. I've been there six years and I train the new operators. I live with my partner Tom, who does bookkeeping and tax returns at a small accounting firm in town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Half my shifts I'm underground in the loader, and the other half I'm in the surface room running a loader by remote control through cameras, which still feels like a video game. Underground it's noise, mud and headlights, and you learn to feel the bucket through the seat. On remote days I can run two stopes in one shift. I love the remote work, and I'm a bit of a nerd about it, I use AI chat tools every day to look up fault codes and plan my study.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A certificate in mine automation, at night, online. I'm about halfway through. The mine pays half the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a pretty quiet future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are still useful, they just didn't change the world. I'd keep using them and not make a fuss. Online I'd probably joke that I'd wasted my time on the certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The mine has another fifteen years, I'm good at my job and the remote side would keep growing slowly anyway. Tom's job would be safe too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the automation certificate and go for remote operations supervisor in a couple of years. Tom and I would keep saving for a house, we've got about three months of expenses saved. I'd keep using AI for study and fault codes, because it saves me time every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything else weighing on you, even in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money's a bit tight since we moved to a bigger rental. Three months saved isn't much, and Tom's firm has had a slow year. Nothing dramatic, just tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the remote side appeal so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's safer and I can do more. Nobody gets hurt in a surface room. And honestly, it's the future of the job either way.

She'd joke online that she **wasted time** on the certificate.
think: The mine has **fifteen years** left and she's good at her job.
Her partner Tom's **bookkeeping job** would be safe too.
do: Go for **remote operations supervisor** in a couple of years.
Keep saving with Tom for a **house**.

fieldNote: She loves **remote loading** for safety and output, not novelty.
Only real pressure is **tight money** after a bigger rental.
Studying **automation** at night, half paid by the mine.

steps.text: Finish the night certificate in mine automation
Save with Tom towards a house deposit
Keep using AI chat tools to check loader fault codes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one I can see clearly. And it worries me more for Tom than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a big shift and people need to start learning now. I'd tell the operators I train to get on the remote shifts early. I wouldn't get political about it, I'd just be practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly good. More remote work, more need for people like me who can run the systems. But Tom's job is checking numbers and filling in tax returns, and that's exactly what the card says goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate faster and push for the supervisor job. I'd sit down with Tom and help him find a course, maybe in financial advice or something with clients face to face. We'd cut back on eating out and hold off on the house until we know where his job's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for me, nervous for us. That's the strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tom take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go quiet. He's already noticed the firm uses software for a lot of the returns. He's the type who worries for a week and then makes a plan, so I'd help with the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Tom's income dropped, could you carry the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes, my pay covers the rent and food. But we'd stop saving, and the house would slip back a few years. That's the real cost.

fieldNote: Her own outlook is good; the risk sits with her **partner's desk job**.

Treats Tom's change as a **joint project**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Two years. Okay, that's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be honest about it, and governments need to move quickly with income support. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. I'd share practical stuff online, like which courses are worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Tom's job is gone in 2028, that's how I'd see it. My remote job is half thinking work too, watching screens and planning, so that goes soon after. And by 2031 the loaders run themselves completely. That's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare dollar, try to get from three months to six fast. I'd get into the team that installs the automation, because there'll be a rush to set it up and they'll need people who know both the loader and the software. I'd also look at moving to a bigger city where there's more work for Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. More scared than I'd show anyone at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're adaptive and you like this technology. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me get the next job, maybe the one after. It doesn't help when there's nothing left to adapt to. That's the bit that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, I'd sell my car and share Tom's. Then the gym, the streaming, all that. And the house is off the table completely.

She'd share **practical advice** online about courses worth doing.

fieldNote: Adaptability **stops feeling like protection** in this picture.
She sees her **remote job** as partly thinking work, so exposed early.
Selling her **car** is the first concrete cut she names.

steps.text: Build savings from three to six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still a sprint, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain if you start straight away, and I'd say that at work a lot. I'd organise a lunch session for the operators on what courses the mine will pay for. Online I'd stay practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives Tom about four years to move into something with people, and me about five to seven years in automation work before the robots catch up. That's tight, but doable. Neither of us would have the jobs we have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate this year and join the automation install team. Tom would start a financial advice course next year while still working. We'd keep saving and maybe buy a small place in a regional city, not here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a busy way. I'd be too occupied to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not buy here, in town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the mine's the only big employer, and if it goes robot, the town shrinks. A regional city has a hospital, a university and more for Tom. Better to buy where people will still want to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, who's 55 and runs the loader I trained on. He's brilliant underground, but he can't stand screens. In five years, he'd be near retirement but not quite there.

fieldNote: She thinks about **where to live** in terms of what survives automation.

steps.text: Finish the automation certificate and join the install team
Get Tom enrolled in a financial advice course next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, now I can actually make a plan I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and people who start now will be fine. I'd keep telling the younger operators to get on the remote shifts and learn the software. Online I'd share what's working for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I'd have years in remote operations, then automation, and by 2039 I'd be one of the few people who really understand the robot fleets. Someone has to be in charge of them, and I'd like it to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the remote supervisor job in the next two years, then a fleet engineering role later. Tom would retrain over a few years without rushing. We'd buy a house around year three, in a regional city with more going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit of nerves, but mostly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that confidence, or hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of both. I can't know the robots won't manage themselves too. But I've always been the person who learns the new machine first, and that's served me well so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger women joining the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the young women joining the mine to get on the remote and automation side early, because there are fewer old habits there. It's a place where you can lead fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tom's job goes first and mine soon after, and there'd be no time to set up anything. What would help is the mine paying for retraining before the robots arrive, and some kind of income support for people like Tom while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about partners. Everyone asks miners about mining, but our household depends on Tom's job too, and his kind of work gets hit first. It's never just one job in a house.
